\begin{abstract}
Latent world models plan by scoring imagined rollouts against a goal
embedding. LeWorldModel (LeWM) trains on a short window of four images
and uses the short-horizon Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) with a Euclidean
terminal cost. When the goal lies beyond one planning horizon, this
cost compares a near-term predicted latent with a still-distant goal
embedding. Existing approaches modify the predictor, the planning
hierarchy, or the distance metric. We instead treat terminal scoring as
a temporal correspondence problem: the two arguments of the Euclidean
cost should refer to the same remaining time. Horizon-Aligned Scoring
(HAS) trains an action-free forward imaginer that maps the short-plan
endpoint toward the goal horizon before the distance is evaluated. On
PushT and TwoRoom, HAS raises mid-range PushT success from $42.8\%$ to
$67.8\%$ and long-horizon TwoRoom success from $16.4\%$ to $70.4\%$.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Latent world models enable goal-conditioned control by scoring imagined
rollouts in representation
space~\citep{hafner2019planet,hafner2020dreamer,hansen2022tdmpc}.
LeWorldModel (LeWM)~\citep{lewm2026} implements this approach with an
action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture
(JEPA)~\citep{lecun2022jepa}: an encoder $E$ produces latent
representations, a predictor $P$ rolls them forward under candidate
actions, and the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)~\citep{rubinstein1999cem}
selects an action sequence using terminal Euclidean distance to a goal
embedding $\zg$.

This terminal cost becomes problematic when the goal lies beyond one
planning horizon. LeWM performs well when the goal is reachable within
a short plan, but at longer offsets CEM must rank short plans by
comparing a near-term predicted latent with a still-distant $\zg$.
Recent work addresses long-horizon planning by lengthening the
action-conditioned
predictor~\citep{du2026vlwm}, planning at several resolutions or toward
predicted
subgoals~\citep{zhang2026hwm,masip2026ffjepa,cheng2026sage}, or
replacing Euclidean MSE with a learned metric~\citep{li2026trm}. These
approaches modify the predictive horizon, planning hierarchy, or
scoring function. We instead study the temporal semantics of terminal
scoring: how should a planner compare a near-term predicted endpoint
with a goal representation from a later stage of the trajectory?

We introduce Horizon-Aligned Scoring (HAS). An action-free imaginer
$F$ learns local temporal transitions from detached LeWM latents using
one-step and recursive two-step supervision. At planning time, repeated
application of $F$ moves each predicted endpoint toward the goal
horizon, and CEM ranks candidate plans by their distance to the goal
embedding at that horizon. HAS thereby separates the action-conditioned
rollout used to generate a short plan from the temporal extension used
to score it.

This paper makes three contributions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Temporal view of terminal scoring.} We formulate
long-offset scoring as a correspondence problem between a predicted
endpoint and a goal embedding associated with different times.
\item \textbf{Horizon-aligned scoring.} We introduce HAS, which uses an
action-free forward imaginer to evaluate short plans at the goal
horizon.
\item \textbf{Long-offset evaluation.} Experiments on PushT and
TwoRoom show consistent gains beyond one planning horizon, including
a TwoRoom improvement from $16.4\%$ to $70.4\%$ at offset $100$.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Latent world-model planning.}
Visual MPC and latent imagination score candidate actions by rolling a
learned model~\citep{hafner2019planet,hafner2020dreamer}. TD-MPC,
DINO-WM, and LeWM use CEM (or MPPI) with a terminal latent
distance~\citep{hansen2022tdmpc,zhou2025dinowm,lewm2026}. In LeWM,
CEM ranks action sequences by Euclidean distance between the predicted
endpoint and the encoded goal.

\paragraph{Extending temporal reach.}
Recent methods extend latent planning beyond a short rollout through
the predictor or the search procedure. VLWM trains an action-conditioned
predictor on variable-length action chunks so $P$ can jump $k$ steps
in one query~\citep{du2026vlwm}. HWM plans at several temporal resolutions
and uses coarse predictions as subgoals for short-horizon
MPC~\citep{zhang2026hwm}. FF-JEPA adds an action-free forward model
that proposes the next subgoal, then runs CEM to that
subgoal~\citep{masip2026ffjepa}. SAGE keeps frozen LeWM and CEM, but
conditions the \emph{proposal} distribution on a predicted
subgoal~\citep{cheng2026sage}. These methods lengthen prediction or
organize search around intermediate targets.

\paragraph{Latent geometry and terminal scoring.}
Temporal straightening regularizes latent trajectories so Euclidean
distance better tracks geodesic progress~\citep{wang2026straightening}.
Trajectory reachability metrics (TRM) replace or combine terminal MSE
with a pairwise head trained on horizon-matched temporal
separations~\citep{li2026trm}. TRM learns a scalar reachability score;
HAS instead transforms the predicted endpoint to the goal horizon and
then evaluates latent distance. The distinction is between learning a
new pairwise metric and changing the temporal correspondence presented
to the metric.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Short-horizon latent planning}
\label{sec:lewm}

Given a four-observation window, the encoder produces
$z_{0:3}=E(o_{0:3})$. The action-conditioned predictor produces
$p_{1:3}=P(z_{0:2},a_{0:2})$, where $p_i$ is trained to match $z_i$.
LeWM combines prediction MSE with SIGReg,
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LeWM}}
=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{i=1}^{3}\|p_i-z_i\|^2
+0.09\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SIGReg}}(z).
\label{eq:lewm}
\end{equation}
During planning, CEM samples action sequences and rolls $P$ forward for
five action blocks. Each block contains five environment steps, so the
predicted endpoint $\Pend$ lies $25$ steps ahead. LeWM assigns the
terminal cost
\begin{equation}
C_{\mathrm{LeWM}}=\|\Pend-\zg\|^2.
\label{eq:lewm-cost}
\end{equation}

\subsection{Learning the forward imaginer}
\label{sec:imaginers}

HAS learns an action-free map $F$ from a predicted latent to the next
encoder-latent time step. $F$ is a two-block residual MLP with latent
dimension $192$ and hidden dimension $768$. Its inputs and targets are
detached from $E$ and $P$, restricting gradients from the forward
objective to $F$.

The four-observation training window provides two one-step pairs and
one recursive two-step pair. We optimize
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{step}}
=\frac{1}{2}\left(
\|F(\bar p_1)-\bar z_2\|^2+
\|F(\bar p_2)-\bar z_3\|^2\right),
\label{eq:forward-step}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{roll}}
=\|F(F(\bar p_1))-\bar z_3\|^2,
\label{eq:forward-roll}
\end{equation}
where bars denote detached tensors. The forward objective is
$\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{step}}+
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{roll}}$. Recursive supervision exposes $F$ to
its own output during training, matching its repeated use at planning
time.

\subsection{Horizon-aligned terminal cost}

Let $o$ be the temporal offset of the goal and $t$ the elapsed
environment steps. After a $25$-step candidate rollout, the number of
remaining action blocks is
\begin{equation}
k=\max\bigl((o-t-\planlen)/5,\,0\bigr).
\label{eq:depth}
\end{equation}
HAS recursively maps each candidate endpoint by this depth and assigns
\begin{equation}
C_{\mathrm{HAS}}=\bigl\|\Fk(\Pend)-\zg\bigr\|^2.
\label{eq:has-cost}
\end{equation}
CEM uses this cost to rank candidate action sequences. As receding
horizon control advances $t$, the recursion depth decreases until
$k=0$, at which point the endpoint already lies at the goal horizon.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:exp}

\subsection{Evaluation protocol}

We evaluate LeWM and HAS on PushT~\citep{florence2022ibc} and TwoRoom
using one epoch-$10$ training checkpoint per task. Evaluation seeds
$42$--$51$ each provide $50$ episodes, with paired starts for the two
methods within each seed. We report the mean and standard deviation of
the ten per-seed success rates.

Goal offsets are $25$, $50$, $75$, and $100$ environment steps. The
interaction budget is twice the corresponding offset. CEM plans five
action blocks of five steps at every offset and replans after executing
the resulting $25$-step action sequence. We use the success criterion
defined by each environment.

\subsection{PushT}
\label{sec:pusht}

On PushT, HAS raises mean success from $42.8\%$ to $67.8\%$ at offset
$50$ and from $21.6\%$ to $40.4\%$ at offset $75$, gains of $25.0$
and $18.8$ percentage points. At offset $100$, success increases from
$13.2\%$ to $23.4\%$. The improvement remains consistent across the
three long-offset settings, while its magnitude decreases with the
offset.

\subsection{TwoRoom}
\label{sec:tworoom}

On TwoRoom, LeWM success falls from $84.4\%$ at offset $25$ to
$42.4\%$, $25.8\%$, and $16.4\%$ at offsets $50$, $75$, and $100$.
HAS obtains $80.4\%$, $82.0\%$, and $70.4\%$ at the same offsets,
corresponding to gains of $38.0$, $56.2$, and $54.0$ percentage
points. HAS improves over LeWM for every evaluation seed at each
offset beyond one planning horizon.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}

The current evaluation covers two simulated tasks and one training
checkpoint per task. It does not yet establish how HAS compares with
longer-horizon LeWM planning or recent long-horizon methods, and
PushT success remains $23.4\%$ at offset $100$. HAS also assumes that
the temporal goal offset is available when selecting the recursion
depth. Broader task coverage, training-seed variation, and direct
long-horizon baselines remain necessary.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:concl}

HAS treats the Euclidean terminal cost of short-horizon latent
planning as a temporal correspondence problem. An action-free forward
imaginer maps the predicted endpoint toward the goal horizon before
distance is evaluated. Over $10$ evaluation seeds, this scoring change
raises PushT mid-range success by $19$--$25$ points and TwoRoom
success at offset $100$ from $16.4\%$ to $70.4\%$. These results
support horizon alignment as a useful design principle for terminal
scoring in latent planning.

at every offset. Training losses and the imagination depth $k$ are
given in Section~\ref{sec:method}. Configurations and scripts used to
produce Table~\ref{tab:main} will be included with the code release.

\appendix
\section{Protocol details}
\label{app:protocol}

CEM uses \texttt{horizon=5}, \texttt{receding=5}, and
\texttt{action\_block=5}, so one plan is $\planlen$ environment steps.
The evaluation budget is $2\times$ the goal offset. Imagination depth
is $k=\max((o-t-25)/5,\,0)$. The LeWM cost is $\|\Pend-\zg\|^2$; HAS
uses $\|\Fk(\Pend)-\zg\|^2$. When $k{=}0$, $F$ is skipped.

Each seed in $\{42,\ldots,51\}$ draws $50$ starts independently. The
numbers in Table~\ref{tab:main} are mean and standard deviation of
those per-seed success rates.

The reported checkpoints were produced by training code that also
instantiates a parameter-disjoint backward auxiliary head. That head
receives detached inputs and is not used by HAS at evaluation; the
forward-head objective is exactly
Equations~\ref{eq:forward-step}--\ref{eq:forward-roll}.
